fr:mainmatter.html:p: A short exact sequence is an exact sequence with all but three consecutive terms being zero. It is often written as 0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0. The short exact sequence describes how B is made up of a subobject A and a quotient C.

Chain complexes arose from combinatorial topology, in the form of a sequence of abelian groups C_n freely generated by cells of dimension n (i.e. encoding the formal sums of cells), and a boundary operator d_n : C_n \to C_{n-1}. The critical feature of the operator is d_{n-1} \mathbin {\circ } d_n = 0, simply written as d^2 = 0, reflecting a deep geometric phenomenon that the boundary of a shape doesn’t have any boundary itself.
A chain complex of abelian groups is given by a sequence of abelian groups G_\bullet together with homomorphisms d_n : G_n \to G_{n-1}, such that d_{n-1} \mathbin {\circ } d_n = 0.
This is eligible to immediate generalization.
A chain complex of R-modules is given by a sequence of modules M_\bullet together with R-linear maps d_n : R_n \to R_{n-1}, such that d_{n-1} \mathbin {\circ } d_n = 0.

Homology can be defined using this algebraic information, without any further reference to topology. Homological algebra is then the algebraic part of reasoning utilized in algebraic topology, repackaged as a stand-alone branch of mathematics. We recall some basics of what we’ve got from algebraic topology.

Given a chain complex, the cycles Z_n of dimension n are given by the kernel of d_n : C_n \to C_{n-1}. The boundaries B_n are given by the image of d_{n+1} : C_{n+1} \to C_n. The equation d^2 = 0 is equivalent to 0 \subseteq B_n \subseteq Z_n \subseteq C_n. We can define quotient groups to measure the gaps in the inclusion chain. By the homomorphism theorem, the quotient C_n / Z_n is isomorphic to the image of d_n, which is the next boundary B_{n-1}. On the other hand, the homology groups H_n(C) are defined as the quotient Z_n/B_n.

Since the boundary subgroup in one dimension can also be considered as a quotient in a lower dimension, it may be beneficial to identify the two in a visualization. This leads to the following picture. Regions appearing to the right are to be considered as quotients, and those to the left as subobjects. Further development of this visualization scheme can be seen here.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We chose to draw circles to emphasize the individual chain groups. In more complicated situations, it is more convenient to draw a chain of rectangles, with each chain group spanning three rectangular regions. We would then need other means to convey the confines of each object.
Given two chain complexes C_\bullet , D_\bullet , the natural notion of morphisms between them is chain maps, i.e. a sequence of maps f_n : C_n \to D_n such that all the squares commute.

fr:title.text: chain maps induce maps on homology

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: chain maps induce maps on homology

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A chain map f : C \to D induces a family of homomorphisms f_* : H_n (C) \to H_n (D) on the homology groups. The identity map induces the identity morphism, and a composition of maps f \mathbin {\circ } g induces composition homomorphism (f \mathbin {\circ } g)_* = f_* \mathbin {\circ } g_*.
Since f commutes with the boundary maps, it maps the boundaries in C_n to the boundaries in D_n. Therefore the map is well-defined after passing to the quotient.
A chain map is a quasi-isomorphism if it induces isomorphisms on the homology groups.
If all the homology groups vanish, then the chain complex is said fo be acyclic or exact. Equivalently, every cycle is a boundary.

A short exact sequence is an exact sequence with all but three consecutive terms being zero. It is often written as 0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0. The short exact sequence describes how B is made up of a subobject A and a quotient C.

Although the definition of exactness and acyclicity are the same, they have different attitudes. Acyclicity reguards the chain complex as a geometric object, concerning cycles and boundaries. On the other hand, exactness takes a purely algebraic perspective, describing how the algebraic pieces fit together.

fr:title.text: Spectral sequence of a tower of fibrations

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Spectral sequence of a tower of fibrations

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a tower of maps X_n \to \cdots \to X_1 \to X_0 = 1, where we assume finite n for simplicity, we wish to compute the homotopy groups of X = X_n from the knowledge of the homotopy groups of the fibers F_n = \operatorname {fib}(X_n \to X_{n-1}).

For each fiber sequence F_n \to X_n \to X_{n-1}, there is a long exact sequence of homotopy groups, and we wish to arrange these information suitably so that knowing \pi _n (F_p) allows us to piece together \pi _n (X). This can be achieved using spectral sequences. See this link for another exposition.

\begin {tikzcd} && {\pi _\bullet (F_{p+1})} && {\pi _\bullet (F_{p})} \\ {} & {\pi _\bullet (X_{p+1})} && {\pi _\bullet (X_{p})} && {\pi _\bullet (X_{p-1})} & {} \arrow ["k"{description}, from=1-3, to=2-2] \arrow ["k"{description}, from=1-5, to=2-4] \arrow [from=2-1, to=2-2] \arrow ["i"{description}, from=2-2, to=2-4] \arrow ["{j^{(+1)}}"', from=2-4, to=1-3] \arrow ["i"{description}, from=2-4, to=2-6] \arrow ["{j^{(+1)}}"', from=2-6, to=1-5] \arrow [from=2-6, to=2-7] \end {tikzcd}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The main difficulty of analyzing the situation is that \pi _n (F_p) is split into two parts that gets appropriated into \pi _{n} (X_p) and \pi _{n-1} (X_{p-1}). This gives multiple possibilities. The case would be easier if, in the rolled-up long exact sequence, one edge of the triangle is always zero. Then the exact sequence splits into various short exact sequences. Since F_p is a fiber, the natural direction is for j to be zero, implying i is epi and k is mono.

To do this, we consider collapsing i to its image, i.e. consider turing i into i' : i (\pi _n (X_p)) \to i (\pi _n (X_{p-1})), repeatedly. From one angle, this makes i iteratively more surjective. From another angle, in the limit, if we consider X_p = X_n where p \ge n, and X_p = 1 where p \le 0 (so F_p = 1 for out-of-bounds indices), then the maps eventually become \operatorname {im}(\pi _n(X) \to \pi _n(X_p)) \to \operatorname {im}(\pi _n(X) \to \pi _n(X_{p-1})), which are surjective. If we still have long exact sequences for these maps, then this produces a filtration F^p \pi _n (X) = \ker (\pi _n (X) \to \pi _n (X_p)) whose associated graded is known.

We have constructed a sequence of exact triangles such that for large enough r, they split into short exact sequences. So now the goal is to give a tractible way to compute the object E_{n,p,r} = \frac {k^{-1} \operatorname {im}(i^r : \pi _n (X_{p+r}) \to \pi _n (X_p))}{j \ker (i^r : \pi _{n-1} (X_{p-1}) \to \pi _{n-1} (X_{p-r-1}))}. As a sanity check, E_{n, p, 0} = \pi _n (F_p), being the “initial condition” for our sequence. Note that this is also the only data we have, as \pi _n (X_p) are all unknown. Therefore we want some way to compute E_{\bullet ,\bullet ,r+1} from the data of E_{\bullet ,\bullet ,r}. (As is the case for all spectral sequences, the “computation” relies on knowing some differentials, but they are often unique by formal reasons.)

Summarizing with the indices aligned with convention, given a tower of maps X = X_n \to \cdots \to X_1 \to X_0 = 1 between simply connected spaces, we have a spectral sequence E^2_{p,q} = \pi _{p+q} (F_q) \Rightarrow \pi _{p+q} (X). With some more work, we can deal with infinite towers and non-simply connected spaces, with sufficiently nice hypotheses.

A homological \delta -functor is a sequence of additive functors T_n : \mathcal {A} \to \mathcal {B} between abelian categories, with the convention that T_n = 0 for n < 0. For every short exact sequence 0 \to X \to Y \to Z \to 0 in \mathcal {A}, we have a connecting map \delta _n : T_n(Z) \to T_{n-1}(X), such that this assignment is natural in the exact sequence.

Similarly, a cohomological \delta -functor can be defined with \delta ^n : T^n(Z) \to T^{n+1}(X). Notice that cohomology does not imply contravariance here. These also have contravariant versions, by replacing \mathcal {A} with \mathcal {A}^\textrm {op}.
